details:
**"The Legend of Sleepy Hollow"**
Irving's most famous story, set in a Dutch settlement near Tarrytown, New York. The superstitious schoolmaster Ichabod Crane courts the heiress Katrina Van Tassel, then vanishes after being chased by the Headless Horseman one night.

**Ichabod Crane, Brom Bones, and Katrina Van Tassel**
Ichabod Crane is the lanky Connecticut schoolmaster in "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow." His rival for the wealthy Katrina Van Tassel is the strong local prankster Brom Bones (Abraham Van Brunt), who marries Katrina after Ichabod disappears and seems to know more about the incident than he admits.

**The Headless Horseman and the smashed pumpkin**
The ghost of a Hessian soldier whose head was shot off by a cannonball in the Revolutionary War, said to ride at night searching for it. After he throws his "head" at Ichabod, only Ichabod's hat and a shattered pumpkin are found the next morning, implying Brom Bones played the Horseman.

**"Rip Van Winkle"**
A story about a lazy, good-natured Dutch villager in the Catskill (Kaatskill) Mountains who escapes his nagging wife and falls asleep for twenty years. He wakes to find the American Revolution has happened, and in confusion he declares himself a loyal subject of King George III at an election, nearly causing a riot.

**Henry Hudson's crew playing ninepins**
While wandering with his dog Wolf, Rip meets strange, silent men in old Dutch clothing playing ninepins in a mountain hollow, revealed to be the ghosts of Henry (Hendrick) Hudson's crew; the rumbling of their game is said to be the thunder of the Catskills. Rip drinks their liquor and falls into his twenty-year sleep.

**The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon**
Irving's 1819–1820 collection, published under the pen name Geoffrey Crayon, containing both "Rip Van Winkle" and "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow." It made him the first American writer to gain wide fame in Europe.

**Diedrich Knickerbocker**
Irving's fictional Dutch historian persona, the narrator of his satirical 1809 A History of New York, which first made him famous; both Sleepy Hollow and Rip Van Winkle are claimed to come from his papers. That History describes the Dutch governor Wouter Van Twiller as "exactly five feet six inches in height, and six feet five inches in circumference." Irving also wrote early pieces as Jonathan Oldstyle.

**"The Devil and Tom Walker"**
A Faust-like story from Tales of a Traveller in which the miserly Tom Walker, after kicking a skull with a tomahawk lodged in it in a swamp, meets the Devil ("Old Scratch"), who has marked trees with the names of the colony's great men. He sells his soul for Captain Kidd's treasure and becomes a usurer, but is carried off by the Devil when he leaves his Bible at home.

**Tom Walker's wife**
Tom's greedy wife goes into the swamp to bargain with Old Scratch herself, taking the household silver in her apron. She never returns, and Tom finds only her apron containing a heart and liver hanging in a tree.

**Tales of the Alhambra**
A collection of sketches and Moorish legends Irving wrote while staying in the Alhambra palace in Granada, Spain. It includes "Legend of the Arabian Astrologer," about King Aben Habuz and a magic weathervane warrior, as well as pieces like "Mementos of Boabdil" and "The Court of Lions"; Irving's guide was Mateo Ximenes.

**Gunpowder and Major André's tree**
Gunpowder is the old plow horse Ichabod borrows to ride to the Van Tassel party; it stubbornly refuses to cross the bridge as the Horseman approaches. On his way home Ichabod passes the giant tulip tree linked to the captured British spy Major John André.

**Dame Van Winkle and Nicholas Vedder**
On waking, Rip learns that his shrewish wife has died after she "broke a blood-vessel in a fit of passion" at a New England peddler. Nicholas Vedder was the village innkeeper whose opinions could be read from how he puffed his pipe, and the inn's portrait of King George has been repainted as George Washington.

**Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus**
Irving's 1828 romanticized biography of Columbus, written while in Spain. It helped spread the myth that educated medieval Europeans believed the Earth was flat. Irving later served as U.S. Minister to Spain and also wrote A Chronicle of the Conquest of Granada.

**Bracebridge Hall and Christmas**
Irving's Christmas sketches about the English country estate Bracebridge Hall (in The Sketch Book and the follow-up book Bracebridge Hall) helped shape the modern American celebration of Christmas.

**Other tales: "The Adventure of the German Student" and "Kidd the Pirate"**
In "The Adventure of the German Student," Gottfried Wolfgang spends the night in Paris with a woman who turns out to be a guillotine victim. In "Kidd the Pirate," the discovery of an old Spanish pistol while fishing leads to stories about Captain Kidd's buried treasure.
